(Lene gives Jakob an old printed sheet from her father, Konrad, who had hidden it under the press for thirteen years: a proclamation “An die Bürger von Mannheim!” that Peter had set in May 1849 and Konrad had printed. The pluperfect (hatte gesetzt, hatte gedruckt, hatte versteckt) is ideal.)
  2. Sie fand einen Fehler: Ein Buchstabe stand auf dem Kopf. (At the bottom Lene finds a typesetter’s mistake: “Maunheim”, an n set upside down so that it reads as u. She says such a mistake happens at four in the morning when one is tired, and that her father did not see it either.)
  3. Er war ein alter Soldat. 1849 war er in der Festung gewesen, zuerst als Soldat und dann als Gefangener. (Brunner is an old soldier who served thirty years in the Baden army. In 1849 he was in the fortress, first as a soldier, then (after the surrender on 23 July) as a prisoner in the casemates. Any answer with these facts is right.)
  4. Wenn ein bisschen Licht kam, las er ein altes Blatt Zeitung vor. Und er lachte laut. (Each evening, when a little light came through the grille, Peter read aloud from an old sheet of newspaper he had hidden in the straw, the same sheet every evening, and he laughed so that all twenty men laughed. wenn (each time) fits the answer.)
  5. Er wollte nach Mannheim, weil seine Familie in Mannheim wartete. (He had heard that a student (Schurz) had got away through the drain; he wanted to get away too, because his wife and his boy were waiting in Mannheim. A weil-clause is ideal.)
  6. Ein Posten aus Preußen hat geschossen, und dann war Peter tot. (Late in July 1849 Peter went into the drain at night. The prisoners, who saw nothing, heard someone in the moat call “Halt!” twice and then a shot; next morning they were told that the sentry, a young man from Prussia who had been ordered that nobody gets out, had shot him, and that he died at once. He lies in a grave for many, without a name, at the back of the cemetery. Do not require an exact place of the shooting.)
  7. Das Parlament hatte nein gesagt, und der König hatte einen neuen Minister genommen: Bismarck. (In Berlin the parliament had said no to the money for the king’s new army, and on the same day (23 September) the King of Prussia had taken a new first minister, Otto von Bismarck. Nobody yet knows what he wants.)

Fragen

  1. Er las einen Satz von Bismarck vor: Nicht durch Reden, sondern durch Eisen und Blut werden die großen Fragen entschieden. 1848 und 1849 waren für ihn der Fehler. (Konrad reads, from the Karlsruher Zeitung’s report from Berlin, Bismarck’s words to the budget committee (30 September 1862): the great questions of the time are decided not by speeches and majority decisions but by iron and blood; that was the mistake of 1848 and 1849. Eisen und Blut is the essential point; the mistake of 1848/49 is a welcome addition.)
  2. Sie würde Bismarck eine Antwort geben, laut, vor seiner Kommission. (Lene would give Bismarck an answer, loudly, before his committee. Then she wants to print an answer in the shop. würde + infinitive is ideal.)
  3. Er wollte sie nicht drucken, weil er nach 1849 gelernt hatte, still zu sein. Er hatte Angst: Die Gendarmen könnten kommen. (Konrad says only students and professors who already agree would read it and nobody in Berlin would see it; above all, after 1849 the gendarmes came every week and he learned to keep quiet, which is why he is still here when many others are not. He would again have to think of the gendarmes every night, and he cannot do that any more. A weil-clause is ideal.)
  4. Ludwig sagte, Bismarck hat recht: Mit Reden macht man kein Land. (Ludwig admires Bismarck’s realism: after years of speeches Germany is still more than thirty states with different money; if it were one country, a Mannheim firm could grow as big as English firms; Bismarck reckons like a merchant. He apologises to Jakob for talking politics, but still believes Bismarck is right.)
  5. Sie hatte das mit dem Kanal gewusst, aber das mit den Preisen nicht. (Since autumn 1849, when a man from Rastatt told her at the door, Kathrin had known that Peter had tried to escape through the drain and had been killed while escaping; she had never known the man’s name. She had not known about the price list Peter read aloud in the casemates. The pluperfect is ideal.)
  6. Er würde den Satz laut und langsam vorlesen, und die Leute würden lachen. (Kathrin says Peter would read the sentence aloud, loudly and slowly, like the prices, like a professor in a lecture, and everyone would laugh; then he would come home and eat his soup. würde + infinitive is ideal.)
  7. Er fragte: Könnten Sie mit Helmholtz nach Karlsruhe fahren? (Kirchhoff asks whether Jakob could go to Karlsruhe with Helmholtz two or three times this winter, for a few days, to build and look after the apparatus for his lectures on force. Bunsen agrees if Jakob does. Jakob says he would like to go.)
  8. Ein guter Sonntag wäre für mich: ein Buch, ein Glas Wein und ein Freund. (Give your own sentence with wäre or würde + infinitive and known words (for example: Ich würde lange schlafen. Ich würde gern nach … fahren.). Any true answer in productive German is acceptable.)

Kapitel 19 · Die Erhaltung der Kraft

Formen

  1. bleibe
  2. sei
  3. habe
  4. werde
  5. wechsle / wechsele
  6. wechselt
  7. brauche
  8. ist
  9. hätten
  10. müssten

Wörter

  1. Schnee
  2. Saal
  3. Gewicht
  4. Wärme
  5. Bewegung
  6. Kohle
  7. Hammer
  8. Batterie
  9. Summe

Fragen

  1. In den Kisten waren Gläser, Zink, Kohle und Draht für eine Batterie. Die Säure trug er in der Hand, weil Bunsen gesagt hatte, er solle sie in der Hand tragen. (The crates hold the battery (four glasses, zinc, carbon), screws, tubes and a thin platinum wire; Jakob carries the acid himself in two bottles because Bunsen told him acid does not belong in a crate. A weil-clause and Bunsen’s words in the Konjunktiv I (sei) are ideal.)
  2. Er sagte, die Lokomotive mache aus der Kraft in der Steinkohle Feuer, Dampf und Bewegung. Das Pferd habe seine Kraft aus seinem Essen. (The locomotive does what the horse does: it takes the force stored in coal and turns it into fire, steam and the motion of the wheels; the horse has its force from its food; nobody makes new force. Reported speech (mache, habe, komme) is ideal; the indicative is acceptable.)
  3. Unter einer Schraube war das Metall grün und schmutzig, von alter Säure. Jakob machte es sauber, und dann glühte der Draht. (A screw contact was green and dirty with old acid, so the current could not pass; Jakob cleaned it with a cloth and the wire glowed. A weil-clause is welcome.)
  4. Er sagte, die Uhr gehe, wenn das Gewicht falle. Wenn das Gewicht unten sei, bleibe die Uhr stehen, und man müsse es nach oben ziehen. (A weight-driven clock goes only while its weight falls; when it is down the clock stops and someone must pull it up again by hand; the force of the hand then waits in the raised weight. Konjunktiv I is ideal.)
  5. Er sagte, das Holz und die Steinkohle seien einmal Pflanzen gewesen, und die Pflanzen hätten ihre Kraft von der Sonne. (Wood and coal were once plants, and plants have their force from the sun; so, Jakob thinks, the morning train ran on old sunlight. seien … gewesen and hätten are ideal.)
  6. Zuerst erzählte er die Worte von Helmholtz. Dann sagte er es selbst, mit seinen Worten, weil er es glaubte. („gehe“ marks Helmholtz’s words, reported (Lene: like the newspaper); Jakob says he believes it and has seen it; when Lene asks for his own words he says „Die Kraft geht nie verloren“, his own statement. A weil-clause is ideal.)
  7. Sie fragte, wo die Kraft von Jakobs Vater sei. (Kathrin asks where his father’s force has gone („Wo ist die hin?“). A reported question with wo + Konjunktiv I (sei) is ideal; quoting her directly is acceptable.)
  8. Mein Vater sagt, Arbeit sei nicht alles. (Your own sentence: a parent’s saying reported with sagt and the Konjunktiv I (sei, habe, gehe, müsse …), or with the indicative as Kathrin does. Any true answer in productive German is acceptable.)

Kapitel 20 · Düppel

Formen

  1. gewaschene
  2. abgelesenen
  3. verteidigte
  4. geschriebene
  5. arbeitenden
  6. stehenden
  7. zitternden
  8. verteidigt
  9. gedruckt
  10. arbeiten / arbeiteten

Wörter

  1. Schanze
  2. Truppen
  3. Zeilen
  4. Feind
  5. Bericht
  6. Bild
  7. Fabrik
  8. Kanonen
  9. Sturm

Fragen

  1. In der Zeitung stand, die preußischen Truppen hätten die dänischen Schanzen bei Düppel gestürmt. (On 18 April 1864 Prussian troops stormed the Danish redoubts at Düppel (the paper says it in one ten-line sentence); many dead on both sides and many prisoners. A plain indicative report is fine; Konjunktiv I/II reporting (hätten … gestürmt) is ideal.)
  2. Sie setzte ‚die‘ und ‚Schanzen‘ mit einem Loch dazwischen. Dann setzte sie die Wörter von Konrad in das Loch. (With metal type she sets ‚die‘, a gap and ‚Schanzen‘; first find ‚die‘, then the word that belongs to it, often at the very end; everything in between says what kind of Schanzen; then she fills the gap with Konrad’s words.)
  3. Der Student wollte nach Hause fahren und sich freiwillig melden. Jakob sagte, sein Vater sei Soldat gewesen; ein Soldat in der Familie sei genug. (Hansen, a student from Kiel, wants to go home and volunteer (two others go too); Jakob says no: his father was a soldier in 1849 at Rastatt, and one in the family is enough. Reported speech (sei) is welcome.)
  4. Er las mit dem Finger, wie Lene es gezeigt hatte: zuerst ‚der‘ oder ‚die‘, dann das Wort, das zu ihm gehört, dann alles dazwischen. (Every evening after work, at home under the lamp, with his finger under the line; on the third evening he uses Lene’s method; he writes a sentence first in his own words and then as Kirchhoff writes (die im Sonnenlicht stehenden dunklen Linien).)
  5. Im Buch fand er die von ihm abgelesenen Zahlen, aber nicht seinen Namen. Er fand auch den Namen von einem jungen Studenten. (Part 1: the two D-line numbers 1002,8 and 1006,8 that he read himself, printed in a list, without his name; already in Part 1 Kirchhoff wrote that the work had made his eyes too tired. Part 2: the name of a young student, Karl Hofmann, who had carried on the work on the map. A participle phrase (die von ihm abgelesenen Zahlen) is ideal.)
  6. Weil Jakob den langen Satz in der Zeitung verstand. Er suchte ‚die‘ und dann das Wort, das zu ‚die‘ gehört, wie Konrad es gelernt hatte. (Ludwig cannot follow the long Gartenlaube phrase; Jakob finds ‚die … Schanze 2‘ and unpacks it (a defended redoubt, defended by Ancker, a Dane), as Konrad says every typesetter must. A weil-clause is ideal.)
  7. Er wollte mit ein paar Bankiers eine große Firma gründen, für Farben aus Teer, Soda und Säure. Ludwig sagte: „Wir brauchen jemanden, der Licht lesen kann.“ (Engelhorn, who makes Mannheim’s gas, wants to found a large firm with some Mannheim bankers: dyes from tar, soda, acid in one factory; Ludwig’s father gives money and Ludwig will work in it. Ludwig ends: they need someone who can read light.)
  8. Am Abend lese ich die Zeitung. Einen langen Satz lese ich langsam, mit dem Finger unter der Zeile. (Your own sentences in productive German: what you read in the evening and how you manage a long sentence. Any true answer is acceptable.)

Formen

  1. wird
  2. ist
  3. sind
  4. wurde
  5. zu

  7. sich
  8. lässt
  9. lässt / ließ

Wörter

  1. Brief
  2. Gäste
  3. Hafen
  4. Wein
  5. Säure
  6. Pläne
  7. Lohn
  8. Ufer

Fragen

  1. Die Kolben waren gewaschen, die Gläser waren sortiert, und die Brenner waren geprüft. Aber Bunsens Kolben war zu waschen; den wusch er selbst. (By eight o'clock the flasks were washed and dried, the glasses sorted, the windows open and every burner tested; only Bunsen's own dirty flask still had to be washed, and Bunsen washed it himself. State passive (waren gewaschen) and sein … zu (war noch zu waschen) are ideal.)
  2. Die Firma ist gegründet. Der Vater von Ludwig lässt Jakob am Sonntag zum Essen nach Mannheim einladen. (The Badische Anilin- und Soda-Fabrik was founded in Mannheim on 6 April (dyes, soda and acid in one firm); they celebrate on Sunday; Ludwig's father invites Jakob to dinner at six; money for the train is in the letter (more than the train costs).)
  3. Der alte Mann erzählte, das Rot sei aus einer Pflanze gekommen, als er jung war; jetzt komme ein neues Rot aus dem Teer. Der junge Chemiker sagte, aus Salz lasse sich Soda machen. (The old merchant: red used to come from a plant and needed many fields; now a new red comes from coal tar (it was unbelievable when he was young; his daughter wears it). Brandt: dyes need acid; soda can be made from salt, but the work needs acid, coal, other substances and a great fire; the new firm makes acid, soda and dyes itself, all in one factory. Reported speech (sei, komme, lasse) is welcome.)
  4. Weil die Stadt Mannheim das Land nicht verkaufte. Eine Firma aus Mannheim bot der Stadt mehr Geld an, und 68 Männer sagten nein. (The city was willing to sell land on the Neckar near the harbour at a good price, but another old Mannheim firm (which also made acid and soda) suddenly offered more; on 12 April the Bürgerausschuss voted no, 68 to 42; Ludwig thinks the rival never meant to buy. Engelhorn went across the Rhine to Ludwigshafen, in Bavaria. A weil-clause is ideal.)
  5. Jakob sagte: Das Laboratorium braucht ein Zimmer, das dunkel zu machen ist, Gas und einen Tisch, der nicht zittert. Dann zeichnete der Chemiker es neu, weit weg von den Maschinen. (A room that can be made dark, gas for the burners, and a table that does not shake, because running machines make the table, telescope and lines shake; on the plan the laboratory stood next to the machines. Brandt redraws it far from the machines, near the water, with a large window; Ludwig: Jakob has had the laboratory redrawn in five minutes.)
  6. Er bot ihm zwölf Gulden in der Woche an, und er schrieb die Zahl auf eine Karte. Jakob sagte nicht ja und nicht nein. (Twelve gulden a week from the first day (three times Jakob's four), and the newly drawn laboratory; he writes the figure and his name on a card: the offer stands, today, tomorrow and in summer. Jakob thinks of rooms, doctor and medicine for his mother, and of Bunsen washing his own flask; he puts the card in his pocket and says neither yes nor no.)
  7. Drüben waren ein paar Lichter von Ludwigshafen zu sehen, und neben ihnen war alles dunkel. Ludwig sagte, Jakob solle kommen und es sich ansehen. (On the other bank only a few lights of Ludwigshafen, then dark fields; Ludwig: there, where it is dark, the factory will soon stand. Jakob: on paper everything is easy, on paper the laboratory is already built. A ship with a red lamp passes. Ludwig ends: “Komm und sieh es dir an.”)
  8. In meinem Zimmer ist das Bett gemacht, und das Fenster ist geöffnet. Aber die Bücher sind zu sortieren. (Your own sentences in productive German about your room: one or two finished states (sein + participle) and one thing still to be done (sein … zu + infinitive). Any true answer is acceptable.)

Kapitel 22 · Ludwigshafen

Formen

  1. daran
  2. darauf
  3. dafür
  4. ihm
  5. damit
  6. ihn
  7. Wofür
  8. Worauf
  9. Womit
  10. dafür

  2. Mitte

  5. Schornstein
  6. Ziegel
  7. Meister
  8. Pause

Fragen

  1. Er dachte immer daran: zwölf Gulden in der Woche. Er erzählte es niemandem. (He kept thinking of Herr Reinhardt's card (12 gulden) while washing flasks and bringing home his four gulden; he told nobody about it, not Bunsen, his mother or Lene; to Lene's „Woran denkst du?“ he said „An nichts … An die Arbeit.“ daran / davon are ideal.)
  2. Ludwig schrieb: Die Fundamente sind gelegt. Komm nach Ludwigshafen! Bunsen sagte: Nehmen Sie den Tag. Er fragte nicht, wofür. (Ludwig: building every day in Ludwigshafen, foundations laid, the first chimney as high as a house; come on a weekday, not Sunday. Bunsen gave the day at once (the glasses are washed, the students can live a day without him), did not ask what it was for, and asked Jakob to look at the burner by the window, whose flame is too yellow.)
  3. Weil die Brücke in der Mitte geöffnet war: Ein großes Schiff mit Kohle kam durch das Loch. (The bridge lies on boats; in the middle two boats with their piece of bridge had moved aside so that a big coal ship could pass; first the ships, then the people. Ludwig adds that nobody crosses when the water is high, which is why an iron bridge is being built. A weil-clause is ideal.)
  4. Er sah Wagen mit Steinen und Sand, Löcher im Boden, Fundamente, Mauern und Schornsteine. Überall waren Leute. (Carts with stone and sand, men digging in pits, long foundations like the plan, some walls as high as a man, and two brick chimneys (one low, one tall with two men on top); in April there had been only dark fields. Ludwig: „Das ist kein Papier mehr.“)
  5. Auf seinen Händen waren weiße und rote Stellen von der Säure. Jetzt trug er damit Ziegel. (Large white and red patches without lines, two fingers he can no longer move properly: acid from a broken barrel in the old Mannheim dye works three years ago. He shows them calmly; he carries bricks with them, no longer fine work. The old firm paid his doctor and gave him work. Any wording for “burned” that the learner knows (Säure, Feuer, kaputt) is fine.)
  6. Er fragte, wofür man das große Fenster braucht, womit man das Zimmer dunkel macht und worauf der Apparat steht. Jakob wusste die Antworten: Mit einem schwarzen Tuch macht man das Zimmer dunkel, und der Apparat steht auf einem Stein. (Window: for sunlight with the mirror and for seeing colours correctly; dark: a black cloth; apparatus: on a stone into the ground, never on wood; gas: one burner and tap for each table, pipes on the wall where they can be seen; soda: a clean platinum wire in the flame, the metals known by their lines (sodium has its lines, potassium others). Jakob learnt it from Bunsen. wo-compounds are ideal.)
  7. Er schämte sich dafür, dass er es wollte. Ludwig wartete auf Jakobs Antwort. (He wanted it: the window, the stone, the twelve gulden, rooms and a doctor for his mother, and most of all the Englishman's questions and knowing the answers; he was ashamed of wanting it and did not know exactly why; he thought of Bunsen not asking what the day was for. On the bridge Jakob only says „Ich denke darüber nach“, so Ludwig is still waiting for his answer (his father can wait, and Ludwig is learning to); Jakob goes home without answering.)
  8. Ich denke viel daran, dass ich nach Deutschland fahren will. Ich warte auf den Sommer; darauf freue ich mich. (Your own sentences: what you often think about (denken an, daran) and what you are waiting for (warten auf, darauf). Any true answer in productive German is acceptable.)

Kapitel 23 · Entropie

Formen

  1. wird
  2. werden
  3. wurde
  4. werde
  5. wirst
  6. würde
  7. werden
  8. wurde
  9. worden
  10. geworden

Wörter

  1. Herbst
  2. Heft
  3. Energie
  4. Entropie
  5. Unterschied
  6. Maximum
  7. Tinte
  8. Grund
  9. Post

Fragen

  1. Im Loch für die Luft saß Salz. Jakob machte das Loch sauber, und die Flamme wurde blau. (Salt (from a student's flame test) sat in the air hole, so little air came in and the sodium coloured the flame; Jakob let the tube cool, cleaned the hole with a thin wire, and the flame turned blue (wurde blau). Bunsen asked only „Salz?“ and did not ask about Ludwigshafen. A weil-clause is fine.)
  2. Er brachte ein neues Heft. Er las die Sätze von Clausius vor: Die Energie der Welt ist konstant, und die Entropie der Welt wird immer größer. (A new issue of the Annalen der Physik with Clausius's paper; Kirchhoff read its last two sentences aloud: „Die Energie der Welt ist constant. Die Entropie der Welt strebt einem Maximum zu.“ Any paraphrase of the second sentence (wird größer und größer) is fine.)
  3. Die Energie ist das, was Helmholtz Kraft nennt. Jakob hat in Karlsruhe gehört, dass die Kraft nie verloren geht. (Kirchhoff: what Helmholtz calls Kraft, Clausius calls Energie; it changes form (Bewegung → Wärme → Bewegung) but the sum never grows or shrinks (konstant). Jakob heard this in Helmholtz's Karlsruhe lecture (Kapitel 19), so he says „Das ist nicht neu.“ New are the second sentence and the word Entropie.)
  4. Der Kolben wird kalt, und die Luft wird ein bisschen wärmer. Auf dem Tisch im kalten Zimmer wird der Kolben nicht von selbst heiß. (The flask gets cold, the air a little warmer; the heat is not lost, it is in the air; on the table in the cold room the flask does not become hot again by itself (in hotter surroundings it would warm up, but that is not the experiment). When heat passes from the warm flask to the cold air, the entropy of flask and air together increases. werden + adjective is ideal.)
  5. Dann wird alles gleich warm sein. Die Energie ist nicht verloren, aber mit der Wärme kann man nicht mehr arbeiten. (Everything will be equally warm, with no difference between warm and cold; the energy is all still there (konstant), but no machine that works with heat, like a locomotive, can do anything with it. Bunsen asks when; Kirchhoff says nobody knows exactly, but not before Sunday, and Bunsen says then he still has time for his line.)
  6. Weil Bunsens Auge am Abend bei der Lampe nicht mehr gut sieht. Es wird nicht besser. (Bunsen's one good eye no longer manages the faint green line by lamplight; the other eye has been bad for many years. He says it calmly („Es wird nicht besser … Es wird nur älter“); in twelve years Jakob had never heard him say he could not do something. A weil-clause is ideal.)
  7. Jakob schrieb: Ich werde nicht nach Ludwigshafen kommen. Einen Grund wusste er nicht. Ludwig war nicht böse. Er schrieb: Du wirst es dir überlegen. (Jakob: he has thought it over and will not come; he cannot give a good reason because he does not know it himself (he crossed out „Professor Bunsen braucht mich“ and the sentence about his mother). Ludwig: not angry, nor is his father; the first acid has been made; the small laboratory will be built anyway and will wait; „Du wirst es dir noch überlegen.“)
  8. Morgen werde ich einen Brief schreiben. Im Herbst werden die Nächte kälter. (Your own sentences: one future with werden + infinitive (ich werde … machen/lesen/schreiben) and one werden + adjective (es wird kalt, die Tage werden kürzer). Any true answer in productive German is acceptable.)

Kapitel 24 · Werbach

Formen

  1. Kampf
  2. Verlust
  3. Einquartierung
  4. Waffenruhe
  5. stellt
  6. verloren
  7. genommen
  8. Preuße
  9. Stadt

Wörter

  1. Nachricht
  2. Gehilfe
  3. Treppe
  4. Dorf
  5. Gefecht
  6. Regierung
  7. Großherzog
  8. Lazarett
  9. Frieden

Fragen

  1. Bei Werbach fand ein Kampf statt. In der Zeitung stand nicht, wer gewonnen hat und wie viele Männer tot oder verwundet waren. (The report says that during the engagement at Tauberbischofsheim a fierce fight took place at Werbach between the Baden division and Prussian and Oldenburg troops, and that the Baden troops fought bravely. It does not say who won (Konrad: then we did not win). A separate report further down, about fighting on the next day (25 July), says the losses of the Baden troops are said to be small; no paper says how many men, and the casualty lists had not come.)
  2. Sie machte aus dem Nomen ein Verb: nehmen. Dann sah sie, wer es gemacht hat: die Preußen. (In official sentences nobody seems to act; there are only nouns. Lene finds the action noun, Einnahme ('a verb dressed as a noun'), turns it back into its verb, nehmen, and the doer appears: die Einnahme der Stadt durch die Preußen → Die Preußen haben die Stadt genommen; here the doer stands after durch. Jakob also looks for the verb first (fand in the middle, statt at the very end).)
  3. Im Telegramm stand: Man stellt die Feindseligkeiten ein; man schießt nicht mehr. Kirchhoff wartete auch auf eine Einstellung der Feindseligkeiten. (Die Einstellung der Feindseligkeiten began at four in the morning the day before, in Italy: nobody shoots there any more. At the Tauber not yet. Kirchhoff, a Prussian from Königsberg who has lived in Heidelberg for twelve years and whose prisms Fritz cleaned, waits for it too; Bunsen says they will wait together. Either a paraphrase with niemand schießt or the noun phrase is fine.)
  4. Die Preußen kamen nach Heidelberg. Ein Preuße schlief bei Konrad und Lene; er war ihre Einquartierung. (Prussian troops (Landwehr: men of thirty and more with work and families at home) marched into Heidelberg on the evening of 1 August. One was billeted with the Hartmanns in the small room upstairs; he was polite, a craftsman from Pomerania with a wife at home, and called himself 'Ihre Einquartierung'. Lene still does not want him in the house.)
  5. Jakobs Gehilfe ist bei Werbach verwundet worden. Eine Kugel ist in sein Knie gegangen, und das Knie wird lahm bleiben. (A doctor wrote it: Fritz was wounded at Werbach on 24 July, a bullet went into his knee, he no longer has a fever, the leg will heal but the knee will stay stiff (lahm), and he will come home in two weeks. Fritz signed his own name. The perfect passive ist … verwundet worden or the future wird … bleiben is ideal.)
  6. Weil die Zeitung schrieb, der Verlust der Truppen war gering. Er war verwundet; er war ein Teil von diesem Verlust. (He read in the field hospital that the losses of the Baden troops were said to be small; as a wounded man he is part of those losses, so with dry humour he calls himself 'a small loss'. A weil-clause is ideal. Bunsen answers by giving him the number book: writing needs no knee.)
  7. Baden musste Preußen 6 Millionen Gulden bezahlen. Kathrin fragte: Wer bezahlt das Knie von Jakobs Gehilfen? (The peace treaty of 17 August fixed a war indemnity of six million gulden, to be paid by Baden to Prussia; the government has already paid most of it, so the Prussians will leave. Kathrin asks who pays for Fritz's knee. Nobody answers.)
  8. Ich habe gelesen: In Amerika haben Soldaten gekämpft. Ein Kampf fand in Amerika statt. (Your own news, first with a finite verb (wer macht was?), then in nominal style (der Kampf, der Verlust, die Einstellung …, with the genitive or durch for the doer). Any true answer in productive German is acceptable.)

Formen

  2. Spektrum

Fragen

  1. Kathrin stand nicht mehr auf; sie lag im Bett, und ihre Hände waren kalt. Der Arzt sagte: Ihr Herz ist müde. (She no longer got up; she lay in bed by the window under a thick blanket, her hands cold, short of breath after every long sentence. Doktor Seitz came every second day and told Jakob on the stairs: weeks, perhaps two months; her heart is tired from many years of cold water.)
  2. Er las einen Text von Kirchhoff vor: In der Sonne ist Natrium. Kathrin sagte: Salz in der Sonne, wie in meiner Suppe. (Kathrin wanted no newspaper ('for the healthy') but 'something of your light'. Jakob read from the 1860 Dingler issue that Kirchhoff had given him: the sentence that sodium is in the sun's atmosphere. He explained it (the same yellow line, bright in the flame, dark in sunlight); Kathrin knew sodium is in salt and laughed: salt in the sun, like in her soup.)
  3. Weil Kathrin nach dem Komma schlief und das Verb vom Hauptsatz lange nicht kam. (The first sentence is very long: after the first comma comes the rest of a long participle attribute, after the second a relative clause (Nebensatz) with its own verb, geworden ist; the verb of the main clause has still not come. Kathrin had asked for it because long sentences are good for sleeping, and she fell asleep; Jakob thought the verb could wait. On the following evenings she slept even earlier. A weil-clause is ideal.)
  4. Sie wollte, dass er Lene heiratet, weil er nicht allein sein soll, wenn sie tot ist. (She asked him to marry Lene ('Heirate die Lene'). She does not want him alone after her death and wants him healthy; whether in Heidelberg or across the Rhine with Ludwig, four gulden or twelve, is all the same to her. Lene has come every evening for five years. Jakob said he would ask her, 'soon'; Kathrin said his father always said soon too.)
  5. In der Anzeige stand: Meine Mutter starb nach langer Krankheit. Jakob sagte: Zuerst kommt die Krankheit, dann sie. (Lene set a printed notice: this morning, after a long illness, my mother Kathrin Lauer, widow of the typesetter Peter Lauer of Mannheim, died; the funeral takes place on Monday 18 March at three at the cemetery. Jakob found the verb (starb, near the front) and saw that the subject came only after the illness. He did not want it changed. Konrad printed fifty copies himself.)
  6. Die Wäscherinnen aus Ziegelhausen, Jakobs Gehilfe, Konrad, Lene, Ludwig und auch Bunsen kamen. Bunsen sagte: Morgen nicht. Die Kolben wasche ich selbst. (Six old laundresses walked from Ziegelhausen; Frau Wendel, Fritz with his stick, Doktor Seitz, Konrad (still weak from fever) with Lene, and Ludwig on the early train (he said nothing of Ludwigshafen). Bunsen, who avoids crowds, came alone on foot, stood beside Jakob, said 'Herr Lauer' and gave him his hand; when Jakob said he would come tomorrow, Bunsen answered that he would wash the flasks himself.)
  7. Er fand das Verb nach einem Komma in der Mitte: Ich habe Beobachtungen gemacht. Das war der Hauptsatz. (Counting the commas (five, 76 words), he found the main clause after the fourth comma: habe ich einige Beobachtungen gemacht. Before it: a joint investigation of Bunsen and Kirchhoff, not yet published, on the spectra of coloured flames, which lets one see what substances a mixture contains; after it: the observations explain the dark lines and let one conclude what is in the sun. Any of these details is fine.)
  8. Ja, ich habe einmal einen langen Satz in einem alten Buch gelesen. Das Verb stand in der Mitte, nach vielen Kommas. (Your own answer, in German you can already use: say where you read it and where its verb stood (am Anfang, in der Mitte, am Ende; nach dem Komma). Any true answer is acceptable.)

Kapitel 26 · Krapp

Formen

  2. sodass / damit

Wörter

  1. Hochzeit
  2. Kirche
  3. Wurzel
  4. Pulver
  5. Alaun
  6. Färber
  7. Bauern
  8. Sauerstoff
  9. Brom

Fragen

  1. Sie hatte Ja gesagt. Aber sie wollte warten, weil Jakobs Mutter tot war, und ihr Vater sollte bei ihnen bleiben. (On the night after the funeral Lene said yes, then: not now; first a year for his mother (a year of mourning), and her father stays with them in his house; she will not leave him, not even with Jakob. Jakob said yes twice, so quickly that she laughed. A weil-clause or a clause with zuerst is ideal.)
  2. Das Rot im Krapp heißt Alizarin. Chemiker in Berlin haben es aus Teer gemacht, und die Firma muss es billig machen. (The red in madder is a substance, alizarin; Graebe and Liebermann in Berlin have made it from coal tar (end of June). It is not a new red like aniline red but the same substance, so new only in where it comes from. Their way is still expensive (bromine); Ludwig's firm must make it cheaply, cheaper than the fields. Then he stopped: not today, it is the wedding.)
  3. Er sah französische Soldaten in roten Hosen. Lene sagte, die Hosen sind mit Krapp gefärbt. (French soldiers in blue coats and red trousers (the Prussians in Heidelberg in 1866 wore dark trousers). Lene: the trousers are dyed with madder, perhaps from her aunt's village.)
  4. Man gräbt die Wurzeln aus, trocknet sie und mahlt sie, sodass sie fein wie Sand werden. (The madder stays three years in the ground; the farmers dig out the roots (not right beside the plant, so that they do not break), dry them in the sun, and in Wasselnheim they are ground fine as sand. The powder, the root and the plant are all called Krapp.)
  5. Das Tuch mit Alaun wurde rot, das Tuch ohne Alaun braun. Jakob sagte, der Alaun und das Rot machen zusammen einen neuen Stoff, sodass das Rot im Tuch bleibt. (Both cloths went into the madder bath; the one laid in water with alum in the morning came out a deep red, the other only brown. Jakob: alum and the red form a new substance that stays in the cloth, so water does not take it away; that is why dyers first lay the cloth in water with alum and then dye it with madder. Odile: a chemist talks like a pastor, he always knows why.)
  6. Sie hatten Alizarin mit Zinkstaub erhitzt. Das Zink nahm den Sauerstoff weg, sodass Anthracen im Glas war, ein Stoff aus dem Teer. (Heating alizarin with zinc dust, the zinc took away the oxygen and anthracene remained, a substance every chemist knew from coal tar: the red of the plant is built on a coal-tar substance, like a house on its foundation. Bunsen reads the sentence aloud from the 1868 Berichte, which has only this first part; the way back (through other substances, with bromine, finally heated with caustic potash) Jakob knows from Ludwig.)
  7. Er sah dunkle Bänder im Gelb und im Grün. Er war glücklich, weil das Licht schnell zeigen kann, ob das Rot aus dem Teer anders ist. (Madder powder in spirit, then a few drops of lye: violet. Lamplight through it showed all colours but two broad dark bands in the yellow and green (scale numbers read for Bunsen, written by Fritz). Jakob hoped the same bands would show the same substance; Bunsen corrected him: the extract holds other substances too, so he needs pure alizarin from the plant and must test both reds the same way; same bands alone prove nothing, but different bands show for certain that it is not the same substance. That night Jakob was as happy as on his first day with Bunsen. A weil-clause is ideal.)
  8. Für mich ist das Schönste das Rot. Ich sehe es gern am Abend am Fluss. (Your own answer, in German you can already use: name a colour or a coloured thing (Rot, Blau, eine Flamme, ein Tuch, das Licht) and say where you see it. Any true answer is acceptable.)

Kapitel 27 · Der fünfundzwanzigste Juni

Formen

  2. sich
  3. treffen
  4. Treffen

  7. führte

Wörter

  2. Probe
  3. Schwefelsäure

  8. Abschied

Fragen

  1. Er hatte reines Alizarin aus dem Krapp gemacht, weil Bunsen es wollte und weil er es Caro zeigen wollte. (All winter, in the evenings after the students had gone, he made pure alizarin from Tante Odile's madder, as Bunsen had advised (first pure alizarin from the plant). He had told Ludwig: an hour with Caro, but only in spring, when he has pure alizarin; without it he can show Caro nothing exact. A weil-clause is ideal.)
  2. Er fand im Blau ein Band, und die Probe war nicht rein. (He compared his pure alizarin with samples A, B and C in spirit with lye: A and C showed the same two bands (which does not yet prove them pure), B a third faint band in the blue, so B certainly holds another substance. Caro: on Tuesday the kettle was too hot; the analyses took four days, Jakob twenty minutes.)
  3. Jakob sollte am Sonntag die Proben prüfen und einen Apparat für die Fabrik bauen. (Caro proposes (einen Vorschlag machen) that Jakob test the week's samples there on Sundays, for two gulden a day, and build a heavy, strong apparatus for the factory; only one man will do for this work (in Betracht kommen). Jakob accepts.)
  4. Anna, die Tochter von Jakob und Lene. Konrad setzte selbst die Anzeige. (Anna was born in the night before Sunday 9 May, a little after three; Frau Wendel helped Lene while Jakob and Konrad waited in the print shop. On Monday Konrad set the notice himself, letter by letter, his hands not trembling this time: two notices in two years, the second easier.)
  5. Die Firma hat in London ein Patent für Alizarin aus Teer angemeldet, ohne Brom und mit Schwefelsäure. Perkin hat sein Patent einen Tag nach der Firma angemeldet. (On Friday 25 June 1869 the firm (Caro, Graebe and Liebermann) filed its patent in London for alizarin from tar without bromine, with sulphuric acid; Perkin filed his on Saturday 26 June, one day later. Ludwig brings the news with a telegram on 30 June, and Caro's letter offering Jakob a post at sixty gulden a month.)
  6. Jakob geht zuerst allein nach Ludwigshafen. Lene, Anna und Konrad bleiben in Heidelberg. (Lene will not have him say he does it for Anna; she made her own decision in March. Her proposal: if he accepts, he goes to Ludwigshafen in August, alone at first, takes a room there and comes home by train on Saturdays; she stays with Anna and her father, who needs her in the print shop; later they will see. Konrad: Ludwigshafen is an hour by train, not America. And: tell Bunsen yourself, soon.)
  7. Bunsen war nicht böse, weil Jakob eine Tochter hat und bei ihm wenig verdient. Er gab Jakob einen alten Brenner. (Bunsen: there is no call to be angry, one has to reckon (a daughter, four gulden a week, sixty a month offered); Jakob need not have waited four years; the decision is Jakob's own, and for a man without an examination no better post is possible at the university. He gives him one of Desaga's old burners from 1855 and says there will always be a bench for him. A weil-clause is ideal.)
  8. Ich habe einmal eine schwere Entscheidung getroffen: Ich habe eine neue Arbeit gesucht und gefunden. Ich habe lange nachgedacht. (Your own answer, in German you can already use: say what you decided (eine Entscheidung treffen or sich entscheiden), and perhaps when or why. Any true answer is acceptable.)

Fragen

  1. Er sah einen langen, hellen Saal mit Schränken voll Glas, und auf den Tischen standen Brenner wie bei Bunsen. (A new hall by the Rhine with six windows, cupboards of new glass, a water tap and a gas tap at every table, his own apparatus on its stone, and on every table a burner like the one Desaga made for Bunsen in 1855: thirty of them, made in Mannheim as many as the firm needed. Any two or three of these details are enough.)
  2. Weil Ludwig 1860 den Arzt für seine Mutter bezahlt hatte. (In 1860 Ludwig paid Doktor Seitz's bill of twenty gulden for Kathrin; Jakob had written it down and never forgotten it. Ludwig had forgotten; he takes the money so that Jakob can sleep calmly. A weil-clause, ideally with the pluperfect (bezahlt hatte), is the target.)
  3. Er fand eine Regel: Wenn der Kessel zu heiß wurde, kam ein Band im Blau, und die Probe war nicht rein. (For three weeks he examined a sample from every kettle every hour and wrote the thermometer reading beside it. Rule: above 190 degrees in the last hours the faint third band appears. His proposal: twenty degrees less, two hours longer; after it there was no third band and more red.)
  4. Caro sagte, dass Jakobs Name nicht darauf steht, weil das Patent der Firma gehört. Ohne Jakobs Untersuchung hätte die Firma den Fehler nicht gefunden. (Jakob's numbers are in the new London patent, but not his name (nor Caro's); at this firm that is always so, the firm pays for the work and the patent belongs to the firm; Caro wanted to tell him himself. Without his examination they would not have found the fault. Jakob gets eighty gulden a month from February and promises to keep the kettle testing secret.)
  5. Der Arbeiter am Kessel war vom Anilin vergiftet. Er fiel auf den Boden, aber er lebte. (Valentin had worked his own shift and a sick colleague's night shift at the aniline kettle; his face was white and his lips blue; he collapsed. Jakob and the foreman carried him into the yard; the doctor said Anilin, a poison. He lived and later worked in the yard with the horses.)
  6. Er schrieb, dass die Färber weniger Krapp kaufen und dass der Preis für Krapp gefallen ist. (The dyers buy less madder than in autumn; they say the Ludwigshafen alizarin will soon be cheaper; the price has fallen a little every month since winter; he asks how much alizarin the firm will sell in 1871 and whether he should still buy madder in autumn. Reported speech with Konjunktiv I (sei, werde) is welcome but not required.)
  7. Weil es ein Geheimnis der Firma war und weil er es Caro versprochen hatte. (How the firm checks its kettles with Jakob's apparatus is a company secret; he had promised Caro. Bunsen did not ask again. Jakob would have liked to tell him (hätte es ihm gern erzählt).)
  8. Ich hätte als Kind Deutsch lernen sollen. Ich hätte auch mehr lesen können. (Your own answer, in German you can use: say what you should have done differently (Ich hätte … sollen), or what would have been possible (Ich hätte … können). Any true answer is acceptable.)

Kapitel 29 · Versailles

Formen

  1. wurde
  2. wurde
  3. wird
  4. wurden
  5. werden
  6. seien
  7. komme
  8. sei
  9. habe
  10. sei

Wörter

  1. Reserve
  2. Strich
  3. Bekanntmachung
  4. Extrablatt
  5. Glocken
  6. Kaiser
  7. Fürsten
  8. Paket
  9. Wohnung

Fragen

  1. Die Männer der Reserve sollten sofort zu ihren Regimentern gehen; ihre Stellen werden freigehalten. Wer das macht, steht nicht darauf. Unten steht: Die Direktion. (The reservists must report to their regiments at once; their posts will be kept open until the end of the war. The notice does not say who keeps them open: no person is named, only „Die Direktion“. A passive (werden freigehalten) or an active paraphrase (Die Firma hält die Stellen frei) are both fine.)
  2. Weil die jungen Männer gingen und weil sein Bruder bei seinem Regiment war. Er ging freiwillig. (Philipp was never a soldier and not in the reserve; he volunteered because „alle gehen“, all the young men, and his brother was already with his regiment; they expected to be home by Christmas. A weil-clause is the target.)
  3. Er brachte ein Paket für einen Gefangenen aus dem Elsass zum Tor der Festung. Der Posten schrieb den Namen auf das Paket. (Odile's son Joseph was taken prisoner at Strasbourg and perhaps brought to Rastatt. Jakob took the parcel (his old coat, shirts, food, tobacco, a letter, a newspaper) to the fortress gate; the Baden sentry wrote the name on it. Jakob saw prisoners in red trousers in the yard and thought of his father, a prisoner there in 1849.)
  4. Er schrieb, es sei kalt, und es komme viel Regen. In der Nacht sei das Wasser Eis. Zu Weihnachten sei er nicht zu Hause. (The newspaper's „nothing new before Paris“ is true, he writes: nothing moves but the rain; in the day rain, at night the water in the trench is ice; he and his brother will not be home for Christmas; greetings to the old man at the gate. Reported with Konjunktiv I (sei, komme) is ideal; direct quotation is also fine.)
  5. Die deutschen Fürsten hatten ihn gerufen. Das Volk steht hinten im Satz; der Kaiser soll seine Kraft größer machen. (In the proclamation the princes and free cities address the call to the king. The people (das Volk) appear only as the addressee of the proclamation and, in the four-part sentence, last, as the object whose strength the emperor will strengthen. Any answer naming the princes, and noticing that the people do not act, is right.)
  6. 1849 hat das Parlament dem König von Preußen die Krone angeboten, aber er wollte sie nicht. Im Reich dürfen die Männer wählen, die Frauen nicht. (In 1849 the Frankfurt parliament offered the crown to the King of Prussia, who refused a crown from the parliament and the people; now the crown comes from the princes; Wilhelm, the brother, came to Baden and Rastatt with the Prussian army in 1849. Still, the Reich's parliament is elected: men may vote from the age of twenty-five, as the 1849 law also said; women may not (Lene).)
  7. Schurz schrieb, er habe in Amerika eine deutsche Zeitung, und Lene könne für die Zeitung setzen. Die Familie entschied: nicht nach Amerika, aber nach Ludwigshafen. (Schurz offered America again, for all of them: setting German type on his German newspaper in St. Louis for Lene, factories for a man who reads light; „die Tür ist offen“. Jakob did not answer for a long time. Lene will not go without her father, Konrad will not cross the sea but can cross the Rhine: they decide to move to Ludwigshafen together, with the press.)
  8. Die Zeitung schrieb, es werde im Winter kalt. Und es war kalt. (Your own answer, in German you can use: report what a paper or a letter said with Konjunktiv I (sei, habe, werde), then, if you like, say in the indicative whether it was so. Any true answer is acceptable.)

Kapitel 30 · Der Hemshof

Formen

  1. wird
  2. werden
  3. wurde
  4. wurde
  5. von
  6. könne
  7. werde
  8. habe
  9. seien
  10. sei

Wörter

  1. Kolonie
  2. Miete
  3. Direktor
  4. Küche
  5. Dach
  6. Garten
  7. Großvater
  8. Nummer
  9. Hausherr

Fragen

  1. Er sah Männer, die lange Gräben gruben. Neben ihnen lagen Ziegel. Hier wurden Häuser für die Leute der Firma gebaut. (Over the wall Jakob saw twenty men digging long trenches for foundations where grass had grown last summer, with rows of new red bricks and a cart bringing more: the company colony is being started. Mentioning the trenches, bricks or foundations is enough.)
  2. Er zeigte ihm auf dem Plan ein Haus mit dem Namen Lauer. Er versprach: Im Frühjahr werdet ihr in diesem Haus wohnen. (A house at the end of the third row with Lauer written beside it; each house has four flats, and theirs is on the ground floor with its own door: a kitchen, two rooms, a small back room with a large window for the press, and the garden behind; walls in autumn, roof in winter, the family will live there next spring; the written confirmation will come from the Direktion. Any answer naming the flat or house and the promise is right; a future with werden is ideal.)
  3. Weil das Haus der Firma gehört und die Lauers der Firma Miete bezahlen, wie einem Hausherrn. (The house belongs to the firm and the family will pay the firm rent, so the firm stands where the landlord used to stand (the Hausherr at Kathrin's door in 1852). Lene says it half joking; Jakob answers „Ein guter Hausherr“. A weil-clause with the verb at the end is the target.)
  4. Er erzählte, seine Familie bekomme eine Wohnung in Nummer zwölf, und das Haus werde vor dem Winter fertig. (Valentin's family gets a flat upstairs in number twelve; the foreman said families with many children come first and number twelve will be ready before winter; four flats, each with a kitchen, a garden for all; he has waited (Wohlfahrt, Kapitel 29) and now knows for whom he carts the bricks. Reported speech in Konjunktiv I (bekomme, werde, habe) is ideal; direct speech is also fine.)
  5. Er hielt einen Draht mit Salz in die Flamme, und die Flamme wurde gelb: Natrium. Dann sagte er zu Jakob den Satz von 1855, und er lächelte. (Bunsen put a platinum wire with salt into his burner flame; it turned yellow and he named sodium. Later he reminded Jakob of his question of 1855 (whose is the burner?) and said, looking at Jakob and Anna and smiling: „Was man weiß, gehört allen. Auch ihr.“ Jakob said yes and believed it.)
  6. Er schrieb, sie blieben am Rhein, und die Firma baue Häuser für ihre Leute. Dieses Haus hätte sein Vater gern gesehen. (After more than a year he finished the letter begun in January 1871: thanks; the family stays on the Rhine; Lene and Anna came with Herr Hartmann in October; a flat in one of the company houses, with a garden and a room for Lene's press, next spring; he does not know either whether his father would have liked that winter, but he would have liked this house; they too have a door now, open to Schurz; Lene adds that she sets type in Ludwigshafen, and well. Reported (blieben, baue) or direct answers are both fine.)
  7. Sie schrieb, ihr Sohn sei zu Hause, und sie habe keinen Krapp mehr gepflanzt. Jakob sah, wie Arbeiter Fässer mit Rot auf ein Schiff trugen. (Joseph has been home since last spring, healthy, still wearing Jakob's old coat; this spring she and the two farmers planted no madder; the dyers of Mülhausen now buy the red from Ludwigshafen; you cannot earn money with madder any more, Joseph says. From the window Jakob saw workers carrying barrels of the tar red onto a ship going up the Rhine towards Strasbourg. Any answer with the madder and the barrels is right.)
  8. Meine Wohnung ist in einer Stadt. Sie hat eine Küche und ein kleines Zimmer. Einen Garten habe ich nicht. (Your own answer, in German you can use: where it is (in einer Stadt, am Rhein …), what it has (eine Küche, Zimmer, ein Fenster, einen Garten) and what it does not have. Any true answer is acceptable.)
